items.item: TPC-H and TPC-DS are presented as a size-and-shape progression (eight tables and twenty-two queries, versus a larger snowflake schema and ninety-nine queries), tying directly back to topic 3's own uniform-versus-skewed and scale-factor material as the same idea at industry scale, rather than as two disconnected facts to memorize.

items.item: ClickBench's own blind spot (no joins at all) is drawn directly from ClickBench's own README, which states plainly that this may give classical data warehouses an unfair disadvantage in its specific benchmark, so the topic treats ClickBench's own documented self-awareness as the source, rather than presenting the blind spot as an outside criticism ClickBench itself does not acknowledge.

at.step: Reveal: ClickBench and its own stated blind spot

items.item: The Join Order Benchmark is connected explicitly, by name, to topic 3's own correlated-column demonstration earlier in this chapter, so a viewer sees the same uniformity-and-independence failure mode scale from one topic's own classroom demonstration to a named, peer-reviewed industry benchmark built for exactly that reason.

at.step: Reveal: the Join Order Benchmark, for cardinality estimation and join ordering

items.item: TPC-DI's obsolete status is verified directly against TPC's own current specifications page at research time, rather than assumed from CHAPTER.md's own planning note, following the project's own never-guess-a-fact discipline, and the topic names what filled the resulting gap (ad hoc or unstandardized ETL benchmarking) without inventing a replacement standard that does not exist.

Benchmarketing and the DeWitt clause are presented as two distinct mechanisms working together, not one: benchmarketing is about which true number a vendor chooses to publish, while a DeWitt clause is about whether a competitor or customer is even legally free to publish a correction, and the topic is explicit that this chapter's own method (an independently reproducible harness) is valuable precisely because it sidesteps both.

at.step: Reveal: benchmarketing and the DeWitt clause

items.item: The chapter-closing lab deliberately re-runs the other three topics' own committed examples.py scripts from this topic's own script, as a literal, mechanically-checked demonstration that the chapter's three artifacts (harness, generator, baseline) are genuinely one reproducible bundle rather than three independent scripts that happen to sit in the same chapter.

The join-order demonstration's own bad-order query is fenced with a MATERIALIZED CTE specifically because an earlier attempt using Postgres's own join_collapse_limit setting showed no measurable difference over small dimension tables (Postgres pushes a selective filter down to a small table's scan regardless of join-reordering settings) — documented in FACT-CHECK.md's Problem Solving section as a real design correction, not presented as if the first approach had simply worked.

The topic is explicit, in CHAPTER.md's own 'Leaves out' line and in this topic's own lab description, that its own join-order query is a disclosed, classroom-scale shape in the spirit of the Join Order Benchmark, never a claim to reproduce JOB's own IMDB dataset or queries, or evidence about any real database engine's production performance.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Every absolute millisecond number this topic prints varies run to run against this sandbox's real, shared Postgres instance, while the qualitative relationship actually taught (filtering before joining is reliably faster than joining before filtering, and the chapter's three scripts reliably re-run clean together) was confirmed stable across two separate runs, which is the property that was actually verified.
